title: The Caliph Omar Bin Abd al-Aziz and the Poets (मराठी)

keywords: the caliph omar bin abd al-aziz and the poets
full_text:
When the saintly Umayyad Caliph Omar bin Abd al-Aziz ascended the throne in Damascus, a delegation of famous court poets arrived from across the empire, expecting to receive rich gifts of gold and estates in exchange for reciting elaborate panegyrics of royal praise.

The poets waited outside the audience hall for three days. Finally, the renowned poet Jarir gained entrance, reciting an eloquent ode praising the new Caliph’s imperial majesty.

Omar bin Abd al-Aziz listened with grave, sorrowful composure. When the verse ended, the Caliph looked at the poet with clear, compassionate eyes:

'Jarir, your verses are beautifully crafted and your meter is flawless. But tell me: from what fund do you expect me to reward you? Shall I take from the bread of the widows of Mesopotamia? Shall I take from the clothing of the orphans of Egypt? Or shall I take from the grain stores of the laborers of Medina? The treasury of the empire belongs to the needy, not to the vanity of the sovereign!'

The poet stood dumbfounded, his heart pierced by the absolute moral integrity of the ruler.

Omar reached into his own personal purse, pulled out fifty silver dirhams of his own private earnings from weaving palm baskets, and placed them in Jarir’s hand: 'This is my own bread, earned by my own labor; take it as a gift from a brother, but do not ask a shepherd to rob his flock to purchase praise.'

Jarir departed with tears in his eyes, proclaiming across all the markets: 'I have met a monarch who fears the heavens more than all the armies of the earth; his justice is the truest poem ever written.'
moral: Public funds belong to the needy; true leaders refuse to spend the people's treasury on flattering verses. [MR]
